source.title: Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity
source.authors: Claire Tian; Katherine Tian; Nathan Hu

page_placements.theme: Enlarging the dictionary adds dead, rare or low-sensitivity latents more than new concepts

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites work on feature splitting and absorption but does not measure splits, feature-to-feature correspondence, or whether child features partition parent inputs. Its own scaling results measure average feature sensitivity, a different property.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions splitting and absorption in related work, but those are cited findings, not results from this study. Its own SAE-width results concern average feature sensitivity; they do not test the claimed splitting behavior.
record.test_reason: The study measures average feature sensitivity, meaning how often a latent fires on LLM-generated text resembling its top activations, across SAE widths and architectures. It never measures splitting, parent–child correspondence, absorption, decomposition into smaller-SAE latents, or concept hierarchies. Splitting, absorption and canonical units appear only as cited prior work in Section 2. Falling sensitivity with width is related to absorption (the authors call absorption a special case of poor sensitivity), but it is a different construct and its cause is not attributed to absorption.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that average feature sensitivity falls with SAE width, in GemmaScope and across 7 SAEBench variants, which they call a new challenge for scaling SAEs. They also find that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates feature sensitivity by generating texts similar to feature-activating examples and measuring activation rates; it does not apply a feature-splitting measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported sensitivity varies with SAE width and sparsity: wider SAEs have lower sensitivity, while higher L0 is associated with higher sensitivity. The paper also reports the width trend across SAE architectures and models.

fits_no_version.finding: Average feature sensitivity falls as width grows. GemmaScope JumpReLU: 0.92–0.94 at 65K vs 0.85–0.87 at 1M. The decline also holds across 7 SAEBench architectures on Gemma-2-2B and Pythia-160M, including Matryoshka BatchTopK.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider SAEs have lower average feature sensitivity (activation rate on text similar to a latent's activating examples), and Matryoshka training does not remove this trend.

record.problems: The width results concern sensitivity rather than splitting. The study filters out rare features and features that do not activate reliably on truncated examples, which the authors note may bias analysis toward common or simpler features. The paper says results across the smaller SAEBench samples are noisier and do not support strong claims about differences between individual architectures.
record.rows_left_out: No results directly measure splitting, feature correspondence, or absorption, so none were extracted as results for V1–V6. Intermediate GemmaScope width values and exact SAEBench width values are shown in plots but are not stated numerically in the text.

untested.parts: Whether coarse latents are replaced by finer latents covering their inputs and lying near their direction as width grows.
Whether splitting occurs in Gemma 2-2B GemmaScope or SAEBench SAEs; only sensitivity is measured in these releases.
Nested, geometrically close feature families mirroring a concept hierarchy.
Whether parent latents fail to fire where child latents fire, and whether size or sparsity changes fix this; no parent/child pairs are identified.
Whether larger-SAE latents decompose into smaller-SAE latents, or whether larger SAEs add novel latents.
Whether splitting is an artifact of the objective; Matryoshka SAEs are compared only on sensitivity, not on splitting.

record.verdict_notes: Rows r1–r3 correctly carry versions ["none"]. One confound matters for any later reuse of the width trend: the 90% truncation filter excludes more features as width grows (51% at 65K to 79% at 1M in GemmaScope). The authors report the trend holds across filter cutoffs (Fig 9) and after frequency reweighting (Appendix C).

versions.untested_parts: Whether larger dictionaries replace coarse features with finer features that cover the same inputs and lie near the coarse feature's direction.
Whether splitting occurs in large models or open SAE releases; the paper tests sensitivity across such SAEs, not splitting.
Whether split features form nested, geometrically close families that mirror a concept hierarchy.
Whether parent features fail to activate when child features activate, or whether changing SAE size or sparsity fixes absorption.
Whether larger latents decompose into smaller latents or add novel latents.
Whether splitting is caused by the SAE objective, or whether Matryoshka SAEs change or reduce splitting. The paper compares sensitivity across SAE widths and architectures instead.

rows.value: 65K width: 0.92 to 0.94; 1M width: 0.85 to 0.87; the text states that sensitivity decreases as width increases.
rows.note: The reported width trend is an outcome for sensitivity, not for feature splitting.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B

rows.value: Wider SAEs consistently show worse sensitivity across all tested architectures.
rows.note: The text reports the direction of the trend; exact values are plotted.

relation.reason: Splitting [4] and absorption [6] come up only in related work (lines 135-137, 151). The results do not bear on any version.

tranche.reason: It measures feature sensitivity across SAE widths and architectures. It never measures splitting, absorption, decomposition or hierarchy, so it does not test any version.

source_check.notes: The row values are correct but they measure sensitivity, not splitting. The GemmaScope 65K and 1M ranges span the SAEs' sparsities. For the SAEBench SAEs (4k, 16k, 65k; L0 near 80) the paper states only the direction of the trend; Figure 8 shows the values. The decline persists after controlling for feature frequency (Appendix C).
